To execrate something means to feel or express an intense, deep hatred or loathing toward it — not ordinary dislike, but a powerful, overwhelming revulsion. Often, this hatred carries a moral weight to it: you don't just personally dislike the thing; you find it fundamentally wrong, evil, vile, or contemptible.

Think of hatred on a scale:

Dislike → Hate → Detest → Loathe → Execrate

Execrate sits at the far end. It is the strongest expression of hatred — full, visceral, and often morally charged.

In its older and more formal sense, to execrate also means to solemnly curse someone — to formally denounce them or call down evil upon them. This isn't about using swear words. It is a more solemn, ceremonial act of declaring that someone deserves punishment or is worthy of condemnation.

These two meanings are deeply connected, and that connection makes the word richer: when you hate someone so intensely that you wish ruin upon them — you execrate them in both senses at once. The feeling and the declaration merge into one.

• "The townspeople execrated the warlord who had burned their homes."

Here, they deeply hate and condemn him with moral outrage.

  • "She execrated violence of any kind, finding it morally reprehensible."

A strong, principled hatred — not just personal discomfort.

  • "The priests execrated the invaders, calling upon the heavens to punish them."

Here the cursing sense is front and center.

  • "History has execrated the names of those who collaborated with the oppressors."

Posterity has condemned them with collective hatred and moral disgust.

Notice how in each case, the hatred is never trivial or mild — it is always deep, serious, and often directed at something considered evil or morally wrong.

Very. And importantly, it's not just about personal discomfort. You wouldn't typically use "execrate" to say you strongly dislike a food, a bad movie, or a rainy day. The word carries a grander, more solemn weight. It is reserved for things you find fundamentally wrong or deeply wicked — cruelty, betrayal, tyranny, moral corruption. The hatred it describes feels righteous, not just emotional.
How Does It Compare to Similar Words?

Abhor — Very close to execrate. Both describe deep hatred. The difference is subtle: execrate tends to have a slightly more public, expressive, and declaratory quality. You're not just feeling it inwardly; you're expressing or proclaiming it outwardly.

Loathe — Similar, but loathe can sometimes be used for relatively minor personal dislikes ("I loathe waiting in lines"). Execrate is rarely, if ever, used for anything trivial.

Abominate — Nearly interchangeable with execrate in meaning. Both suggest deep moral revulsion. They can usually be swapped without changing the meaning significantly.

Detest — Slightly less intense than execrate, and it lacks the moral-condemnation quality that execrate carries.

Curse — Captures the second meaning of execrate, but "curse" is a much more casual, everyday word. Execrate in that sense is more solemn and formal.

The direct opposites of execrate are words like revere, venerate, adore, extol, and laud — all of which involve deep admiration, praise, or respect. Where you execrate something you find evil and worthy of condemnation, you revere something you find noble and worthy of honor.

A helpful mental contrast: think of execrate as the dark, solemn twin of celebrate. To celebrate is to publicly honor and praise something with joy. To execrate is to publicly condemn and despise something with moral outrage.

Execration (noun) — The act or state of execrating; extreme hatred, moral condemnation, or a solemn curse.
"The dictator's name became an object of universal execration."

Execrable (adjective) — Something so bad or vile that it deserves to be execrated; shockingly terrible or of the lowest quality. This is actually the more commonly used word from this family — you may encounter it more often than "execrate" itself.
"The conditions in the dungeon were execrable."
"The speech was execrable — dishonest, cruel, and poorly reasoned."

Execrably (adverb) — In an execrable manner; appallingly badly.
"The prisoners were execrably treated."
Register and Context — When Is This Word Used?

Execrate is a formal, literary word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation — it would sound unusual and overly grand if someone used it casually. It appears most naturally in:

  • Literary prose and serious fiction
  • Historical, philosophical, or political writing
  • Formal speeches or moral essays
  • Religious or classical texts

In everyday speech, the same idea would be expressed as: "I detest this," "I find this utterly revolting," or "I abhor this." Execrate carries a grander, more elevated register that suits formal writing better than casual talk.

If you had to capture the full spirit of the word in one sentence, it would be this:

To execrate something is to hate it with the deepest, most morally charged revulsion possible — and often, to say so openly and solemnly.

It is the language of righteous condemnation. When history execrates a tyrant, when a community execrates an act of cruelty, when a writer execrates injustice — the word is doing more than expressing a feeling. It is passing a verdict.
